(CNN) — After nearly 150 years in business, the *Rocky Mountain News* published its final edition Friday, becoming another casualty of a troubled economy and the rise of the Internet era.

The Denver, Colorado, newspaper’s last front-page headline was simple: “Goodbye, Colorado.”

“It is with great sadness that we say goodbye to you today. Our time chronicling the life of Denver and Colorado, the nation and the world, is over.”

The newspaper’s owner, E.W. Scripps Co., announced the decision to the newsroom at noon Thursday, ending three months of speculation and uncertainty about the paper’s future. The *News* had been put up for sale in December.

The *Rocky Mountain News* is the latest victim in an era of shutdowns, layoffs and cutbacks afflicting the newspaper industry.

“It’s in a free fall and nobody knows where the bottom is. It’s kind of like water in the toilet swirling around and nobody knows what’s left when you’re done flushing,” media critic Eric Alterman said.

Newspapers across the country are under mounting pressure as readership declines and advertising revenue falls, while increasing numbers of Americans turn to the Internet for information.

“All newspapers are under great pressure. They’ll survive, but they’ll survive in different forms, their costs base will have to be dramatically lowered,” said Mort Zuckerman, publisher of the *New York Daily News*, which has the seventh-highest circulation in the country.

The sharp decline in advertising revenue amid a brutal economy has forced newspapers to cut costs by laying off cartoonists, columnists and other staff members, leaving many to search for work in an already struggling industry.

Pia Catton lost her job as arts editor of the *New York Sun* five months ago, when the newspaper closed. She has since taken a short-term position editing a book, but said she may soon need to consider other career paths.

“There will always be a market for news, you will always need to know immediately what’s happening. Will there be a market for newspapers? That’s another question,” she said.

The *Rocky Mountain News* had more than 200 editorial employees, according to the Columbia Journalism Review’s website.

Rich Boehne, chief executive officer of Scripps, told employees the newspaper had fallen victim to a severe economy, upheaval in the newspaper industry and multimillion-dollar annual losses.

“Denver can’t support two newspapers any longer,” Boehne said. “It’s certainly not good news for you, and it’s certainly not good news for Denver.”

Since 2001, the *News* had been in a joint operating agreement with *The Denver Post*, combining the papers’ business operations in an effort to save money while keeping their editorial departments separate. The closure of the *News* leaves Denver with one major newspaper, as is the case in most American cities.

“We’ve been, sort of, hanging on the edge for so long,” said Mel Pompanio, a presentation editor for the paper. “What a huge loss for Colorado today.”

This week, the *San Francisco Chronicle* announced that it was at risk of being sold or closed unless it stops losing millions of dollars. Officials from Hearst Corp., which owns the *Chronicle*, said the paper lost $50 million in 2008 and is on pace to lose even more this year.

“It’s difficult. It’s hard,” said Lynn Bartels, a political reporter and 26-year Scripps employee, speaking about the *News* closing. “I haven’t returned any phone calls yet, because I don’t need to be reporting and crying at the same time. I’ve done that enough.”

Video posted on the newspaper’s website showed somber faces throughout the newsroom. A few sobs could also be heard as the announcement of the closure began to sink in among employees.

“I could say stupid things like ‘I know how you feel.’ I don’t,” Boehne said. “We are just deeply sorry. I hope you will accept that.”

CNN’s Richard Roth contributed to this report.

Newspapers nationwide are facing mounting strain as both readership and advertising income fall, while increasing numbers of Americans turn to the Internet for news and information.

“Every newspaper is facing enormous pressure,” said Mort Zuckerman, publisher of the New York Daily News, the newspaper with the seventh-largest circulation in the United States. “They will survive, but in different ways, and their cost structures will have to be reduced substantially.”

A severe recession and a sharp drop in advertising revenue have pushed newspapers to lower expenses by laying off cartoonists, columnists and other staff members, sending many into a difficult job market within an already troubled industry.

Pia Catton, formerly the arts editor at the New York Sun, lost her position five months earlier when that newspaper shut down. She has since taken temporary work editing a book, but she believes she may soon have to consider other professions.

“There will always be demand for news; people will always need to know right away what is going on,” Catton said. “Whether there will be demand for newspapers is a different issue.”

According to the Columbia Journalism Review’s website, the Rocky Mountain News employed more than 200 people in its editorial department.

Rich Boehne, Scripps’ chief executive officer, told staff members that the paper had been hurt by a disastrous economy, major disruption within the newspaper industry and annual losses totaling millions of dollars.

“Denver can no longer sustain two newspapers,” Boehne said. “This is certainly not good news for you, and it is certainly not good news for Denver.”

Since 2001, the News had operated under a joint operating agreement with The Denver Post. The arrangement merged the two newspapers’ business functions to reduce costs, while keeping their editorial staffs independent.

With the News gone, Denver is left with one major daily newspaper, as is the case in most U.S. cities.

“We’ve been kind of living on the brink for such a long time,” said Mel Pompanio, a presentation editor at the paper. “This is an enormous loss for Colorado today.”

Earlier in the week, the San Francisco Chronicle said it could be sold or shut down if it failed to end its multimillion-dollar losses. Representatives of Hearst Corp., which owns the Chronicle, said the newspaper lost $50 million in 2008 and was on track to lose even more during the current year.

Video posted on the newspaper’s website showed a newsroom filled with somber expressions. Some crying could also be heard as employees began absorbing the news that the paper was closing.

“I could say foolish things like, ‘I know how you feel.’ I don’t,” Boehne said. “We are simply deeply sorry. I hope you can accept that.”
